Here’s what it looks like to love people generously without running empty.", "author": "699e12d16ef041f10a195450", "item-category": "69c092cd5c80cc7ef09d9860", "tabs": [ "69c09dca3cac7986ad2990b4", "69c33aae5e60542e77d08f86", "69c49e12beca94b04b361ec1", "69c085d28383a3710d83adf6", "69c085ddd46b33b7eed0d1f7", "69c22206c7ede1d4fc6a5fa1", "69c09000d8c5e5cbe7c9eca5", "69c09000d8c5e5cbe7c9eca5" ], "main-content": "

I burned out once. Not dramatically — no single moment I can point to. It was a slow erosion: too many people, too little margin, a growing feeling that I had nothing left to give but kept trying to give it anyway.

I tell this story because it's relevant to any honest conversation about love. If love costs something — and I believe it does — then the question of how to sustain it matters. A lot.

Because the answer to burnout is not to love less. But it is also not to ignore the fact that you are finite.

John's gospel records Jesus saying something that has stayed with me: “Abide in my love.” Not “work harder at love.” Not “overcome your limitations through sheer effort.” Abide. Stay connected to the source. The image Jesus uses immediately after is a vine — you don't produce fruit by straining; you produce it by staying attached.

I've been in San Francisco long enough to have watched people arrive full of conviction and leave exhausted. The city is beautiful and demanding. The needs are visible and large. The gap between what is and what should be is wide enough to disappear into.

The answer to burnout is not to love less. But it is also not to ignore the fact that you are finite.

What I've come to think — slowly, and still imperfectly — is that sustainable love requires knowing who you are when you're not giving anything to anyone. It requires returning, regularly, to something that restores you. For me that's baseball, long walks with the dog past SFMOMA and down to the waterfront, and conversations with people who ask how I'm actually doing.

Paul, writing to the Romans, describes a kind of love that is genuine but also wise — one that hates what is evil and holds fast to what is good. This is not reckless. It is rooted. It distinguishes between enabling and loving, between self-abandonment and sacrifice.

There's a version of love that is generous because it is secure — not because the person doing it has unlimited resources, but because they know where to go when the reserves run low. That seems like the kind of love that can actually last.

I don't think I've solved this. I still run too fast some weeks and too slow on others. But I'm more convinced than I used to be that loving people well over time requires being honest about your own limits — and finding, regularly, what actually fills you back up.

That's not a small thing. It might be the most important thing.
